clinicalPearls: A subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia in which blasts show megakaryocytic differentiation, historically designated AML-M7 in the older French-American-British classification.
Blasts express platelet and megakaryocyte antigens such as CD41, CD42b and CD61; myeloperoxidase is characteristically negative, which can mislead if only routine cytochemistry is used.
Marrow is frequently fibrotic (reticulin fibrosis), so aspirates are often a dry tap and adequate diagnosis may require a trephine biopsy with immunohistochemistry.
In children with Down syndrome it is strongly associated with somatic GATA1 mutations and, following transient abnormal myelopoiesis of the newborn, generally carries a favourable prognosis.
Down-syndrome-associated disease is notably chemosensitive and is treated with reduced-intensity regimens to limit toxicity.
Non-Down-syndrome paediatric cases often harbour recurrent fusions such as RBM15-MKL1 (OTT-MAL) or CBFA2T3-GLIS2 and tend to behave more aggressively.
In adults it is uncommon, frequently arises against a background of myelodysplasia or as therapy-related disease, and generally has a poor outcome.
Cytopenias, marrow failure and hepatosplenomegaly are common; organomegaly and myelofibrosis are more prominent than in most other AML subtypes.
reference.pathophysiology: Acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia results from clonal proliferation of immature cells committed to the megakaryocytic lineage that fail to mature into platelet-producing megakaryocytes. Distinct biological subgroups exist. In children with Down syndrome, constitutional trisomy 21 combined with an acquired truncating mutation in the transcription factor GATA1 (producing the short GATA1s isoform) first drives transient abnormal myelopoiesis in the neonatal period; in a proportion of infants, additional cooperating mutations in cohesin and signalling genes lead to overt leukaemia in early childhood. In children without Down syndrome, recurrent chimeric fusions such as RBM15-MKL1 and the cryptic CBFA2T3-GLIS2 aberrantly activate megakaryocytic and stem-cell transcriptional programmes. Megakaryoblasts and their progeny secrete fibrogenic cytokines including platelet-derived growth factor and transforming growth factor beta, stimulating marrow reticulin and collagen fibrosis that accounts for the frequent dry tap. Blasts retain megakaryocytic surface glycoproteins (the fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor receptors) enabling immunophenotypic identification, while marrow replacement produces the anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: Other acute myeloid leukaemia subtypes, including acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis
Transient abnormal myelopoiesis of Down syndrome (neonatal, self-resolving)
Metastatic small round blue cell tumour infiltrating marrow (in children)
Acute panmyelosis and other causes of a fibrotic dry-tap marrow
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow trephine biopsy with reticulin staining given the high rate of dry tap
Flow cytometry for megakaryocytic markers CD41, CD42b and CD61
Immunohistochemistry for platelet glycoproteins and von Willebrand factor on the trephine
Cytogenetics and FISH, including testing for CBFA2T3-GLIS2 and RBM15-MKL1
GATA1 mutation analysis, particularly in infants and children with Down syndrome
Full blood count with film and coagulation screen
Baseline organ function and imaging for hepatosplenomegaly before treatment
redFlags: Severe pancytopenia with bleeding or life-threatening infection
Features of disseminated intravascular coagulation or spontaneous haemorrhage
A newborn with Down syndrome and marked leucocytosis or organomegaly (possible transient abnormal myelopoiesis or progression)
Signs of leukaemic infiltration or tumour lysis at presentation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly context-dependent: Down-syndrome-associated childhood disease is chemosensitive and usually carries a favourable outcome with reduced-intensity therapy, whereas non-Down-syndrome paediatric cases with high-risk fusions and most adult cases have a considerably poorer prognosis. Adverse cytogenetics, therapy-related or myelodysplasia-related disease worsen outcomes.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because myeloperoxidase is negative; lineage assignment depends on megakaryocytic immunophenotyping, not myeloperoxidase.
Reporting an aspirate as inadequate or hypocellular without proceeding to a trephine, missing fibrosis-obscured blasts.
Applying standard high-intensity AML regimens to Down-syndrome patients, causing excess toxicity.
Confusing neonatal transient abnormal myelopoiesis, which often resolves spontaneously, with established leukaemia.
Overlooking cryptic fusions such as CBFA2T3-GLIS2 that require targeted molecular testing to detect.
